utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Vujic, yesterday afternoon we spoke about the two psychologists or perhaps a psychiatrist in Germany who you wished to call as well the psychologist here in Holland. As I indicated, the Trial Chamber had read the report of Dr Nedopil and we really did not understand your purpose in calling him. I don't know what it would add. He examined Mr. Tadic, as I recall, while he was in custody in Germany, so that was three and a half years ago or so. Let's see. Here is the report. I don't have the exact date. In any case that was before he was transferred to the Tribunal here in April of 1995. I gather he has not examined him since. So I am wondering what is your purpose of calling him. As we indicated in the June 12th order the Chamber preferred written reports but if it was necessary we would hear oral statements as well as receiving a written statement. So I don't know the purpose of calling him. With respect to the psychologist here in Holland, we all reviewed that report yesterday evening. The psychologist examined Mr. Tadic in July of 1995, and having read the report, I also do not understand the need for that psychologist to appear and state what is in her report. So would you please respond to those concerns that I have?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is true that yesterday we discussed that, that an expert appears before this court, a psychiatrist or a psychologist, one of those who examined the accused, Dusko Tadic, so that we would receive information based on the verified findings of the tests carried out, so that we would get the necessary explanations that are not contained in their written findings and opinions. When we talked about the Dutch psychologist, we only said that if Professor Nedopil could not come before this court because of the time that you established for having him heard, that we hear this psychologist instead. However, since I have been informed by the Victims and Witness Unit that it was agreed with Mr. Nedopil that he would come on Friday and that he would make it here by Friday, 10.00 am, that is to say the date that you established in your order of June 12th, I feel it is necessary to hear Professor Nedopil not so that we would establish his ability to understand his actions -- that is a psychologist is usually required to do -- but we would like Professor Nedopil to explain how he came to his findings as to the personality of Mr. Dusko Tadic. Of course, the Defence has many other additional questions in terms of Mr. Tadic's character and how he came to certain conclusions, and that is why we insist on having Mr. Nedopil brought before this court and heard before this court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You had originally filed a request for a continuance of this sentencing, stating that Dr Nedopil would not be available. It was then in the Order -- you are correct -- state if he was available prior to July 4th, we'll hear him. We'll hear him and we will be able to see whether, in fact, after he testifies he has added anything to the report which we have and have read. We will hear him and then you will not be calling the psychologist, I gather, from Holland.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I truly cannot establish at this point whether there will be supplementary information needed but I do expect certain additional information and additional opinions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Do you intend calling the Dutch psychologist, Dr de Man-Roorda?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: No, your Honour. We will be satisfied once we have heard Mr. Nedopil.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Then we will hear from Dr Nedopil. I understand that he will be here on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you, Mr. Vujin. You may call your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the Defence do that, may I raise just a couple of matters? Firstly, I understand that the two exhibits that we tendered yesterday have not as yet been allocated a number, and just continuing on the numbering system that we had applied during the trial, the next two numbers would be 371 and 372. P371 can be the investigator's declaration of Robert Reid dated 17th June 1997, with the attachment A being the affidavit of Hakija Elezovic, and perhaps P372 can be the investigator's declaration of Thomas Akhavan, dated 17th June 1997. Just following on from what has been said by the Defence this morning and their intention to call the witness on Friday, I don't know whether the proceedings will then go on into next week, but if that occurs, unfortunately I have a difficulty for the following two weeks after that, so somebody else from the Prosecution would have to take over in that event, if the proceedings went on in those two weeks, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: One other matter. There was one other matter which was causing confusion for the Prosecution with respect to the report of Dr Nedopil you mentioned. When you refer to the report, are you referring to the complete report of some 33 pages of Dr Nedopil, or are you talking about the two page extraction which the Defence submitted as part of their documents to the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: All we have is what the Defence submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: All right, your Honour. We were just not sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: If there's a fuller report, perhaps we should have that before Dr Nedopil testifies. That would give us some assistance perhaps in understanding his testimony. Do you have a longer report or do you just have a two-page report, Mr. Vujin?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: We have a complete report by Professor Nedopil, but we thought that it was not necessary at this point to burden the court with the entire report, given the circumstances, but we can submit it to you, but only in the original German language, because we don't have a translation, in as many copies as you wish. We have four copies of the entire material, but I don't think it is needed, because it also contains certain information that we are not going to discuss before this court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: We have the English translation of the complete report here, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Provide Mr. Vujin with a copy of the translation and we will take a recess at 4 o'clock, and if he has an opportunity to review it and accept that that's a proper translation, then it could be admitted after the recess, or perhaps even tomorrow. So that ends that. Give Mr. Vujin a copy of the English one and then we would like copies of it, if that's acceptable to the defence, if that's a proper translation. We judges have been discussing the scheduling concerns. You have five additional, six additional witnesses; is that correct, Mr. Vujin?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: We have two witnesses -- three witnesses for today and we also proposed and expect to have Professor Aleksic invited, too. So that would mean four witnesses altogether. We believe that can all be completed today. Then it remains to be seen what will be done tomorrow and the day after tomorrow, but we believe at any rate that we can finish on Friday, after having heard Professor Nedopil, and that probably will not take longer than an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You then believe you will be able to complete -- you have four remaining witnesses and you will be able to complete all four of them today, certainly tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: I imagine -- certainly by tomorrow. Certainly tomorrow, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Is it possible to receive your oral submissions, on oral submission from the Prosecution and an oral submission from the Defence, as well as if Mr. Tadic wishes to speak -- he may wish to speak after Dr Nedopil -- is it possible we go forward with the submissions from Prosecution and Defence, submissions from counsel, regarding the appropriate sentence, and then hear Dr Nedopil on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: As far as the Defence is concerned, we are prepared for such a schedule, but perhaps we would say a few words about what Mr. Nedopil would say on Friday, but that wouldn't take very long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We are of the same position, your Honour. As long as we can say a few things, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: As long as we don't have any days not working because we want to work every day. When we complete the four witnesses, they will hear submissions from counsel. Then we'll hear Dr Nedopil on Friday. That will be some time after 10.00 am on Friday because we have an initial appearance on Friday before that. Then if you say additional words in light of Dr Nedopil's statement, oral statement, then each side will be permitted to do so. Okay. Mr. Vujin, you may call your next witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. The Defence calls upon witness Nikola Petrovic, who will be examined by my colleague, Mr. John Livingston -- Mr. Kostic, I'm sorry. Mr. Nikola Petrovic (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. You may be seated. Mr. Kostic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Examined by Mr. Kostic

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Your name is Nikola Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where do you live, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I live in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By training I'm a cook. I completed a higher school for cooks and now I work as a policeman in the local prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you trained to be a police officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1982 in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have been a police officer since that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since then I have been working as a police officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (Inaudible) KP Dom. Would you explain to the Tribunal what that is exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: KP Dom, Banja Luka, that is the name of this institution, that is to say with the persons who are imprisoned and detained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In some other countries the name for police officers who do those kind of functions are corrections officers. You are familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was a different name in our country, too, but during the war and after the war we got a different name. Policeman of the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As such an officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long have you known Dusko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was first here before this court I said the same thing, that I have known him since 1975.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have known him either on a weekly or monthly basis since 1975?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The tide of life took me to one side, him to another side, but we were friends. Until 1978 or 1979 intensively we were seeing a lot of each other and from 1979 until 1980 something we didn't see each other that often, but we did keep in touch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were school friends also; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he's older than I am. His wife and my wife are school friends and we are friends from the club. We were involved in sports together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How is your wife employed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She works in a medical laboratory. She works in the hospital in Paprizo in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With regard to being friends with regard to sports activities, would you tell me a little bit about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were together in this sports club and we trained together with his brother Ljubo Tadic, who was in charge of the club. We were involved in sports outside the club, too; athletics, for example. We would lift weights, etc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you belong to a particular club?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that club, the Borac Karate Club.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where does that name come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Borac. In Banja Luka there are several clubs called Borac in Banja Luka: football, handball, basketball. The karate club is also called Borac. Borac is somebody who fights in a ring, a stadium, etc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you achieve yourself some level of status in your sport?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Together with them and with their help as a young man I won an award in karate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (Inaudible).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the First Dan black belt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me about the karate that Mr. Tadic was involved in both in terms of the physical type of karate as well as if there is any philosophy that goes along with that type of karate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is Ludarju style. In Banja Luka there were several clubs that were called Shotokan style, Ludarju. We chose this one. I came to that club by accident and I liked the people and the way in which they were treated, the coach and the people who trained there, so I stayed on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now you have testified earlier that you began to see Mr. Tadic more frequently some time in 1989/1990; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me about the frequency of your meetings with Mr. Tadic once we went to 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We would see each other every now and then, not that often, when he would come to Banja Luka, he would try to come to see me, too. Also I had relatives in Sanski Most. So I would travel by his home and I would stop to see him. Quite often I would also come to his cafe, to his home. I admired his success, first and foremost, the things he created in his life, his prospects, etc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (Inaudible).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He wanted to take care of his family financially. He managed to earn enough money for the cafe. He was talented. What can I say. I was involved in sports in Kozarac. I said that before, that he also had a club there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever visit the cafe that Mr. Tadic was operating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me about the atmosphere? Was there anything particular about the music, the decorations in the cafe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The music was for young people only to the best of my knowledge, what young people enjoyed listening to at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was decorated very nicely, the cafe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know anything special. I didn't notice many things then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it showing nationalistic slogans or some other things of that nature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't notice that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now there came a time when Mr. Tadic had an unfortunate situation where a window was broken in his cafe. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the last time I visited him or the time before that. I can't remember exactly. Before the SDA party was established, that was the majority party in Kozarac. As the minority in that town, it is only natural. There were people -- I don't know how to put this -- people could couldn't stand people who were of Serb origin. I'm not trying to say it was everybody, but there were individuals who in a way hated Serbs, and during our conversation somebody threw a stone at his cafe and there was a letter, a sort of a letter wrapped around the stone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm just having a problem with the set, the ear set. Mr. Petrovic, we don't want to go into all of the details about that particular incident, but I just wanted to know whether you discussed this particular incident with Dusko. Tell me what his reaction was to that incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We talked about that. He didn't react -- he didn't overreact to it. He wasn't very disturbed by it. He thought that it was only an individual who did it, that it wasn't a mass of people who did it and this wasn't out of personal hatred towards him. Somebody threw it. I don't know. It wasn't established who it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you that he wanted to get some type of revenge against this person who did that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'm going to sort of focus your attention to a period of time in 1992 and tell me how frequently you met with Mr. Tadic during that year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just said so. Before the fighting in Kozarac we would see each other a couple of times say in 20 days or in a month, and when the fighting broke out in Kozarac and that area, Dusko escaped to Banja Luka and we would see each other every day and sometimes every other day, but at any rate we would see each other frequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you discuss the events and activities that happened in Kozarac at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every time we would see each other it was a normal visit. We would go out for a drink, and then we would talk about what happened to your house, what happened to your cafe, how are you faring here, where do you live, what are you going to do in the future. That was the kind of conversation we had. He didn't have a way out of that situation then. Something had to be done, and he didn't know what, because the times were such, because you imagine that you can do something one day and the next day you are simply lost.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his attitude about what was happening there at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was sorry, because he lived for Kozarac and he lived in Kozarac as far as I know. He was sorry that things happened the way they did. I'm saying this in all sincerity. He was sorry for his friends and he had many Muslim friends there and also some Serbs who fled from there, who had to flee. He felt sorry for them, too, but what could he do? He was sorry about everything that had taken place there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if he made attempts before the conflict to try to prevent that conflict in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you in my view Kozarac was led by a political party, and he could not do anything about it, because he was a national minority there, and it seems to me that in some way these people were deceived, these Muslims, too, because -- I mean, this is my personal opinion, because they accepted this kind of dual -- these kind of orders from I don't know who.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you about the circumstances that Dusko Tadic found himself in 1992, and you saw him regularly. Did you have discussions with him about the fact that there was going to be a general mobilisation of all men to become members of the army of Republika Srpska, and what was his attitude about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The mobilisation started immediately, first of all, voluntary mobilisation, and after that under orders of the Banja Luka Court, that is to say that all people who were able for military action received call-up papers and were supposed to go to their war posts, and those who didn't have such posts, and there were a lot of people who were in hiding because, of course, there were a lot of people who didn't want to go and get killed from all sides, not only from the Serbian side, they went into hiding. Muslims, Croats and a lot of Serbs, too, didn't want to go and fight the war. Among them was Dusko also because at that time he was staying in Banja Luka, as I already said. I personally had to hide him on one occasion because a military patrol came by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. You are telling us about a military patrol. What was the method of mobilising people in Banja Luka at that time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, can you establish a date when he is referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am interested in a time that would be 1992, when you were seeing Mr. Tadic on a regular basis, and I would say that would be between the end of May through June, July and August of 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The methods of mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mentioned that, first, a call-up document was sent by courier, and people who did not respond to this document, military police patrol would come to his house to pick him up. If he was not home, if he was caught in the street, then the military patrol asks for his ID, which requires showing your military identification card with a stamp indicating the war unit you belong to. Those who don't have such ID documents are usually arraigned, put in a military van and taken to military custody. They were given uniforms, given weapons and sent to the front, where the fighting was worst.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there also situations where the military police would just surround an area and question all males between the ages of 20 and 50, let's say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That would happen regularly in the market place. We were trying to earn some money for a living at the market, and me and Dusko saw each other often there. They would simply surround the market place. There would be three or four patrols, and they would carry out their controls or checking of able-bodied men from 20 to 50, 60. Then the procedure follows, as I have just said. You have to show your military ID papers. If you don't have them, you go to the front.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had occasion to hide Mr. Tadic from such procedures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On one occasion I concealed him because he didn't have any papers. I managed to hide him and later on he went to his brother's, Ljubo, or wherever he was staying. I was never there so I don't know exactly but he went to his apartment. When he saw there was no choice after all that he had to report somewhere to have a wartime assignment, and as far as I know, he found some connections, somebody who had a position high up, who sent him to Prijedor to be a traffic policeman, because, of course, it was difficult to get such a post, just to keep watch duty on the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any of your discussions with Mr. Tadic did he tell you why he did not want to be mobilised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't want to be mobilised myself and neither did he. After all, it's much nicer to be with one's family. He simply didn't want to go to war, as far as I could understand him. Some people volunteered even to wage war, but he didn't have the slightest inclination. He felt no hatred for anyone. He never saw any point in that war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is what he told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now you continued your relationship with Mr. Tadic into the later part of 1992, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have discussions with Mr. Tadic about his desire to leave Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On one occasion I visited him in Prijedor to see how he was getting on and where he was living, and we talked. After that, after those exchanges of visits, he came to Banja Luka again, and he talked to me, because my sister is in South Africa, and he asked me to give him her telephone number so that he could contact her to move and settle there, because he had lost his father in the meantime and, of course, as far as I heard, he had problems with the Prijedor authorities. I don't know whether the flat belonged to a company or the municipality, but he was being thrown out and he had to leave the apartment, and his house in Kozarac was damaged -- I know that; I saw it -- so he didn't have any place to go. If you are there, you have to go to war, but you've got to do something. You have to have a wartime assignment, and if you're at war you have no income. What are you going to live off?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (Inaudible) period of time when Mr. Tadic returned to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He returned to Kozarac I think it was -- I think I saw him at the beginning of 1993, the first half of 1993, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he doing in Kozarac at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time I think he held the post of secretary of the local commune of Kozarac, but he hadn't moved into his own house. He was living in Prijedor and he was travelling there, at least when I went to visit him. He went to Kozarac on a daily basis to his office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have conversations with him at that time, and that's early 1993, whether he wanted to remain in the Republika Srpska, or had a desire to leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We talked. He didn't see any future for him there. He wanted to go somewhere, but he didn't know where.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Eventually he left Kozarac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he came to Banja Luka again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have contact with him at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were his plans at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His plans were, as I said, to -- he wanted to go to South Africa. He called my sister up a couple of times, but it was difficult to get the necessary papers. Then later on he decided to go to see his brother, Mladen, who was in Germany. I don't know in which town exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Throughout 1991, 1992 and 1993, were you working at your position at a police officer -- correctional officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware through your contacts that Dusko Tadic was arrested in regard to his failure to answer the call for mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know he had some problems in Prijedor, that people were jealous of his post of secretary of the local commune, and it was only normal, because one group of people were going to war and getting killed, and there he is sitting in his nice office, and then they, as far as I know, demanded that he go to the front.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your years as a police officer and a correctional officer you had an opportunity to know about criminal matters, who was arrested, who the people are who tended to cause trouble in that area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness nodded.)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that Dusko Tadic was arrested for a violation of the laws?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also know a lot of people, and my question now is framed really in a time period for all of the years that you've known Mr. Tadic. You have talked about Mr. Tadic with other people, have you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he has a certain reputation in his community, does he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is his reputation in regard to his ability to be law-abiding, not to cause trouble, not to violate the laws?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Banja Luka there was a lot of talk, because it is a small town, about the Tadic brothers, who had clubs in Germany, Banja Luka, Prijedor, Kozarac, and only the best things were said of them, as far as I know. In Kozarac, too, we had a number of sports meets, and I went there and I saw that there too he had a high reputation. He was respectable. His family, his father was deeply respected by the local people, by the local Muslims in Kozarac. Therefore, the whole Tadic family was highly respected. It was not known for any violations of the law, for being quarrelsome or in any way doing anything bad. They led a normal life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have spent through all of those years a lot of time with Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You socialised with him. You were in public places with him, and, of course, through your competition, you attended those events; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mr. Tadic lose his temper, get involved in a fight, or threaten people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never noticed anything like that. I know when he was training with his own brother it was done in a sportsman like spirit. The two of us never had this kind of sports training between ourselves. We never had a fight, a sports fight, so I think he was a good sportsman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is not just in regard to athletic contests but also with regard to his behaviour with you in public, in public places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were never any problems because I never wanted to make -- cause problems myself, and Dusko was a modest man. We led a quiet life. If we went out, we went out with girls. We didn't wish to compromise our reputation by causing any difficulties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having the ability to spend time with Mr. Tadic, particularly the last few years, 1992/1993, all the events that occurred in that part of former Yugoslavia, do you have -- do you know from talking to Mr. Tadic and observing him how did he react to all of those events sort of in the final analysis when it was all over?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally can say what I thought, and I can speak on his behalf, that he was horrified by certain things that were happening. He felt that was he to join in anything, as a secretary of the local commune, that he could maybe make some improvements, but, as I said, the first time there was euphoria was widespread on all three sides. I'm not defending either side. If the world and the international community had not prevented it, I don't know where it would have led. As for Dusko, he also looked upon all of this with horror, because -- and he didn't like it, of course, because he wanted to go from there. He wanted to escape, because he didn't find his way in those surroundings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan? Cross-examination by Mr. Keegan

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Mr. Petrovic, in your testimony today you stated that you had admired Dusko Tadic and his success in the Kozarac area the things that he created for himself, and you stated that you admired that he had managed to earn enough money for his cafe. Are you aware that he borrowed that money from Muslims from Kozarac, those same Muslims who he then helped to cleanse from the area and imprison in Omarska and Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: It is a multiple question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I will overrule your objection. Can you answer that question, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't get the translation at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That solves that problem. You can break it down and translate it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can hear now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The first part was to ask if you recalled your testimony. Are you aware that Dusko borrowed the money to start that cafe from Muslims in Kozarac, the same Muslims he helped to imprison in Omarska, Keraterm and Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also stated that you knew that Dusko Tadic did not want to be mobilised into the armed forces. Are you aware that, in fact, Dusko Tadic did serve with the forces that attacked Kozarac and cleansed the Muslims, killed Muslims and imprisoned them in camps in the Prijedor area?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: I have an objection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko Tadic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Excuse me. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: I think again it's a multiple question. The other thing is that it was my belief that the culpability issue was not going to be examined here, and I think both of the questions have asked that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. Well, the involvement of Dusko Tadic in the attack on Kozarac --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Do you wish Mr. Petrovic to take off his earphones? That is the procedure we followed during the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I don't think it is necessary. That has been established by the court --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can testify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Just wait one moment. Counsel now are discussing questions with me really.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: -- in its findings, and so I'm simply using that fact to test the basis for this witness' opinions and assertions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I'll overrule your objection, Mr. Kostic. Now Mr. Kostic says it's a multiple question. He can answer "yes" and we don't know whether he's answering "yes" to the first part or the second part. That's an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The first part is not actually a question. It is simply the recollection of the witness' testimony. The question is: are you aware that he participated in the attack and the actions that occurred in that attack?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. That's the first part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: That's the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Go ahead. Can you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember Dusko Tadic did not participate in the attack on Kozarac, because at that time he was in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes. Not going with your testimony the first time you were here, today you spoke of an occasion that you had to give Dusko Tadic shelter from some raids in Banja Luka, when the police were trying to round up men who were avoiding the mobilisation. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no attack on Banja Luka. They were the military police forces for mobilisation who carried out such operations on virtually a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Today you testified that on one occasion you had to hide Dusko Tadic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We were sitting in a cafe and I had to hide him so that he wouldn't get mobilised because he didn't want to be mobilised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in your previous testimony before this Tribunal you, in fact, never mentioned that. Your only testimony was that when raids started for men of military age who were to go to the front, Dusko Tadic fled and returned to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He first fled Kozarac and came to Banja Luka. He hid in Banja Luka for a time. I know very well what I said the first time. Dusko Tadic hid for a long time escaping mobilisation. He didn't want to go to war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also stated today that the traffic police position was a difficult position to get, that he must have had some connection in order to get that job. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The position was a part of the police force and there were many checkpoints in those days. Through certain connections -- I don't know the name of the connection, I know it went through somebody who appointed him to that post, so he would have some kind of a wartime assignment, because this was counted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think it's possible that he got that position as a reward for his service on the attack on Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Objection. Asked and answered. I think he is asking a very speculative question without any foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. This witness has testified, one, that he is a police officer for fifteen years. He has testified now that he understands it requires some sort of connection in order to get such of a job. He also testified he knows the Kozarac area and Dusko Tadic very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I really don't think his opinion will help the Chamber. I will sustain the objection. You need not answer the question, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I would prefer you not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In light of that, I will not ask any additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, you are excused permanently. Thank you for coming again to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, too. (Witness withdrew from court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin, would you call your next witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. The Defence calls Ms. Mira Tadic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Would you please read the declaration that has been given to you, Ms. Tadic? Ms. Mira Tadic (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, you may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Examined by Mr. Vujin

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Ms. Tadic, this is the second time that you appear before this court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember your testimony the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you still abide by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Tadic, today we would like to hear from you certain things that you were not asked then and things that you perhaps mentioned only in passing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are interested in your family relationships, your family -- your relations in the family in the broader sense, how you see your husband. We are interested in what you know about his activities, and that is why we are going to take things in a certain order. How long have you been together with Dusko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean married or how long we've known each other?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long you have known each other. When did you marry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We met when I was 15 and when I was 18 I married him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you marry him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 17th April 1979 -- August. August. I'm sorry. I got confused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please calm down a little bit. We understand the situation, but we need some of these specific data. Where did you live after you got married to Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the family home in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Whose house was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The family home of Dusko's father.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of Dusko's father. Did you live together with Dusko's father and mother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in a joint household.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the relations between you as the daughter-in-law and them as the parents-in-law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We got along very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your attitude towards them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I also appreciated them and I respected them and liked them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We already said that Dusko Tadic's father died; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what state of health is his mother now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She is ill. She is hardly mobile.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are you by training?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A nurse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you still on good terms with the mother and family of Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, basically I'm the one who is taking care of her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Dusko's father's attitude towards his sons? We know that Dusko also has three brothers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He took great care of them. I would say that he was even over-protective of them. He cared for his children immensely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the attitude of the children towards their father?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They loved him and respected him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Was there ever any quarrelling between Dusko and his father or you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the relations between and among the brothers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good as long as the father was alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after the father died?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were certain tensions because of property affairs, in terms of sharing the property.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this handled eventually?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who raised the issue of property?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was raised by his brother Mladen [Redacted) (redacted). That is what it was basically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted) (redacted). Does Mladen still live in Kozarac today?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I object to the question and the answer about another witness in these proceedings and I would ask that there be a redaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: It was answered by other witnesses, too, but I think the court can hear about these facts from this witness also and this can be of importance. I don't see why facts should not be checked through the statements of all witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, my understanding of these proceedings is we will hear evidence from witnesses about the character of Mr. Tadic and that's the purpose of it and the purpose of that evidence is to assist your Honours in determining any sentence that you may ultimately impose. It has nothing to do with any other witness or any other person that has had any connection with these proceedings other than Mr. Tadic, and I strongly object to the defence bringing up issues relating to other witnesses who have testified before these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Who mentioned what? Last time I also said that when I examine a witness, I ask the witness questions that I'm interested in. I'm interested in relations within the Tadic family, the relations between the brothers, so that you would get the impression of the family that he comes from, so that you would see what kind of person he is, so that you could decide on the sentence, if that is what is supposed to be done. So if the witness is answering something, the Defence has no way of knowing what the answer is going to be. So this kind of objection of the Prosecutor is unfounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Yesterday we did have a concern about witnesses coming --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: I insist on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: -- Coming to testify about the character of Mr. Tadic and using that opportunity either intentionally or perhaps unintentionally to cast dispersions on witnesses who have testified during the trial. Now that should not be done. The question that you asked was: what were the relations like between the brothers and the answer was that there were tensions after the father died. That ended the answer really. Ms. Tadic then volunteered that they were started by a brother and then at the insistence -- so I don't know the answer was called for by Mr. Vujin, but Mr. Vujin, would you please, as you confer with your witnesses as they come -- before they come to this hearing, make it very clear to them that the purpose of the hearing is to hear about Mr. Tadic and not to refer negatively for whatever purpose they may wish to about witnesses who have testified, and, Ms. Tadic, since you are hearing this discussion, you understand what I am saying. We would very much like to hear from you giving your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: -- About the character of your husband and any other matters that may help this Trial Chamber in determining the appropriate sentence but witnesses who have previously come to testify are not on trial, and there is really no need to mention them. So the answer is yes, there were tensions after the father died between the brothers, but it is totally irrelevant who caused those tensions, and certainly when you mention a witness who has come --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: -- There is a concern on the part of the Prosecutor. If you will, please refrain from those kinds of responses. Thank you. Go ahead, Mr. Vujin.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Ms. Tadic, who lives in the family house of the Tadic’s now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko's brother with his wife and children and mother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is Mladen's wife's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Suzanna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What nationality is she?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She's Catholic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Tadic, after your daughter Valentina was born, how was she named?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She was named by my late father-in-law. She was named after Valentina Triaskova, who was the first woman astronaut.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your father-in-law bring his children up in such a way so as to respect all nationalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now that we mentioned the name, it just came to my mind. I want to ask you: how did you call Dusko in the family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dule.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a nickname, a term of endearment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dule is a term of endearment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What kind of a husband and father was Dusko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For me a very good husband and father. That means that he was caring, he was always attentive and caring. He took me to nice places. He would buy everything for me and my daughter. He helped me with the housework.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Enough for me. Did he help you with all housework when you were present and absent? Did he take care of the children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did take care of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he do everything? Was he ashamed to do some of the women's chores?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He did women's chores and he didn't do some of the men's chores. For example, he would never cut up the firewood. He would never slaughter a chicken for me. On the 29th, when we would slaughter pigs, he never took part in that. It was very strange to me, because I come from the rural areas and it was the man of the house who was supposed to take care of that. My father would always do that, for instance, but we always had to call somebody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Tadic. Before the events and during the events in the Prijedor Opstina and after that you always accompanied your husband?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me before these events was Mr. Tadic interested in politics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have certain political activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, only in the pre-war period when Yugoslavia fell apart. Only then we had such activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Organising the plebiscite.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Organising the voting for the plebiscite?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was when you were appointed a member of the committee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the municipal commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you for a moment, Mr. Vujin. Regarding the prior objection that was established, Mr. Niemann, the redaction will be granted. You may continue, Mr. Vujin.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Tadic, are you aware of the facts related to the activities of your husband as a member of the Red Cross, as a secretary of the local community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me when the local community of Kozarac started working again and who was involved in this restoration of activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Activity was restored by my husband; Bosko Dragicevic -- can I mention other names? I don't know. With some other people, Serbs, from Kozarac. This started some time in August 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Could I now tender certain documents on the restoration of the activity of the Kozarac local community? We have some more documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: It is not fair that you perform all of the functions, Mr. Vujin. We have two people here to help you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: I have five copies.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Is this the decision restoring the local community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: This document has been numbered what exhibit? We will number them consecutively from the Defence's exhibits at trial as well, as the Prosecutor has. We were going to renumber all those. This would be what? THE CLERK OF THE COURT: This would be document D108.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: The next document, we are supposed to show it, it has a signature on it. This is the next document. Ms. Tadic, do you recognise the signature on the original document in the Serbo-Croat language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is not the original document. It is a photocopy. Yes, I recognise it. It is the signature of my husband. You can't see it very well but I recognise it to be my husband's signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your husband's signature. Thank you. The next document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Ms. Tadic, that's your husband's signature. Does that exhibit have a number on it? Is that 109?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There should be a number but you can't see the exact number here. It is a poor photocopy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Turn over on the back of it, Ms. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That's 109?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you. That's your husband's signature then on that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: The document that you're looking at now, is that decision to set up the local committee of the Red Cross in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this decision passed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 11th November 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does the decision say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That the members of the local committee of the Red Cross are appointed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is your husband there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, under number 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As the member of the committee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell me what your husband, Mr. Tadic, did within his activities as secretary of the local community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As secretary of the local community his duty was to bring life back to Kozarac to the extent possible, to repair the waterworks, the sewage system, the post office, the medical centre, to bring a doctor there, to help people who stayed on, to receive food through the Red Cross. That was it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the conflict was the medical centre in Kozarac damaged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the building still there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your husband succeed in restoring the medical centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the health service start working after that regularly? Do you remember a doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Doctor Lazman, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. As a Red Cross activist and secretary of the local community did Mr. Tadic have the obligation to take care of the population that returned to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what way and what did he organise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For example, he organised for them to have a Red Cross office there, to receive food, and these people, refugees, who came from Velika Kladusa, it was his duty to help them, to help them in resolving certain questions in that commune.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did Dusko Tadic decide who would be coming in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was people who came there collectively. He was supposed to take care of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To take care of them once they were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one more document from this part of the testimony. Could we submit another document, please? Ms. Tadic, please have a look at the signature on the page before the last, at the very end.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have three signatures there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you read the text?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, just the handwriting. On the day of 25th November 1992 humanitarian aid was distributed according to the document of November 1992, 356 persons. Signatures: 1, Jokovic Daniella; 2, Chedo; 3, Tadic Dusko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The third signature is that of your husband?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. To go back now to the time before the conflict that broke out in that territory, did your husband take part in a delegation of the people of Kozarac, and if you know about this, what kind of a delegation was that? Where did they go and what did they do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I wasn't present. I was in Banja Luka then, but he told me about it. He went with a committee on behalf of the local community of Kozarac to Prijedor. It mostly consisted of intellectuals from Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of what nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your stay in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I don't want to interrupt the Defence all the time. We have heard this evidence from Mr. Tadic. Are we really going to be assisted by having repeated what he told her and she comes here and tells us again something which he has already told us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I'll overrule your objection, Mr. Niemann. You may proceed, Mr. Vujin.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Ms. Tadic, after the conflict, when Mr. Dusko Tadic managed to join the traffic police as a reserve policeman, you went back to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm interested in knowing whether at that time in Prijedor there were still some Muslims who were living there amongst the population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you and your husband communicate with some of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We continued being friends with them, as we were until then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you take medicine to some of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can't remember. Yes. Thank you. These contacts, were they normal, just like before the fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any unpleasant situations with the authorities of Republika Srpska or the authorities at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time let me tell you it was risky, frankly speaking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get an apartment in Prijedor in that period or in the following period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you live in that apartment and for how long?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We lived there for about a year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then we were moved out of that apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moved out? Could you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That means that we were evicted, that we were thrown out of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who threw you out of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The authorities in Prijedor at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because my husband was not on the front. We couldn't keep it. Then it's only the warriors and people wounded in the war who obtained apartments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that is why you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and the situation is the same now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then we went to a private apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A private apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your husband ever receive any kind of reward for his work from the Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can one speak of the attitude of the authorities towards you as a good attitude or were you persecuted in a way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was a kind of persecution after all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us go back a bit to your life and to what you know about your husband in terms of obligations. Do you know whether after he did his military service, whether your husband ever went to any military exercises?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many mobilisations there were before the conflict and during and in the immediate aftermath?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many times there were a mobilisation in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean before the fighting in Kozarac? What are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the fighting, after the fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was general mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I know that. The first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time in May 1992 when everybody had to respond.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was still in force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was still in force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your husband respond to this mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which way did he manage not to respond the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time simply because he was not listed in their records, so they didn't pick him up, and the second time he avoided that because he was in the traffic police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this an award or through the help of relatives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it wasn't an award. It was done through various connections, as people say in our country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was this connection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Radovan Vokic, a relative of his.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether your husband was arrested because he didn't respond to mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was arrested on two occasions. I was present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would also like to submit the things we mentioned yesterday. This is from the office of the Public Prosecutor and the court in relation to criminal proceedings instituted against Dusko Tadic. Are you aware of the fact that criminal proceedings have been instituted against your husband before a military court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document, is that what it shows?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Tadic, during your life with Mr. Dusko Tadic did you try to go abroad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, many times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For what reasons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For purely economic reasons. At the beginning they were purely economic reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the conflict when did you go to Germany?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 1st August 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We couldn't go on there any more. We went to Germany because my husband wasn't in the army. I had nothing to expect there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your husband was persecuted. You were persecuted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My husband was supposed to go into the army, so I would have some kind of status in Republika Srpska, and he didn't, so that was that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the period in Banja Luka did he manage to find a job as refugee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not in Banja Luka because there were mobilisation. I had to report to my own duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your stay in Germany did you also decide to go abroad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We talked about that. We tried.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get documents for going to Canada?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the document that you obtained in Germany in the intention of going to Canada?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Vujin. If you are going to another area of questioning, perhaps now is a good time to take a recess. Before we do that, you have had marked defence exhibits 108, 109, 110, 111, 112 and now 113. Do you wish to admit those -- wish to have those admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Yes, the Defence would tender them as evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: They will be admitted and the exhibits that were marked yesterday for the Defence, I presume there is no objection. If they are without objection, they are also admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: We will stand in recess until 4.20. (4.05 pm) (Short break) (4.20 pm) (Witness re-enters court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Ms. Tadic, I should like now to go on to another area, the last one, but before I do that, let us return for a moment to the activities of your husband regarding the revival of life and work in Kozarac linked to the medical centre. You said that you know that the centre was damaged, but the building as such still stood. When you are saying it was damaged, do you mean that all the medical equipment was taken away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where it was taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the medical centre in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because at that time he was working at the medical centre in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All our things were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your husband at that time come to intervene? You saw the letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To talk to the general manager of the medical centre in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he come on several occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have any difficulties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course he had difficulties. They were never restored to Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they went on using that equipment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It went elsewhere. It was taken away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did he manage to get something, some of the basic instruments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A minimum of things, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago we were talking about Muslim families that stayed on in Prijedor, and that you kept in touch with them. You couldn't remember taking medicines to anyone. If the Trial Chamber permits me: Mejobez Lugic and his wife, who was disabled; Elvis with a five-member family. Do you know these names, these families?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. May I just add, if any one of these people contacted me and if I was able to help, I would, and I considered that normal.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The interpreter would like to ask that the questioning slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Do you know whether your husband provided permits for movement for these families?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does that mean? Were they able to move around freely? Were special permits required or were these granted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I hear there is a problem in the interpretation booth.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: It's very fast. I will slow down. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. At that time in Prijedor and in the surroundings was movement allowed freely or were special permits required from the competent municipal authorities for movement of people and things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Certain permits were required. People who fled from Kozarac, if they didn't have the necessary documents they needed new certificates with the help of which they could be identified, because raids were frequent in town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Dusko Tadic help these two families to get those documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to tender for identification one such certificate, which has to do with the movement of Dusko Tadic, and please I would like you to identify it. Were those documents of this kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a certificate on the basis of which your husband could take some things out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, only on a basis of a certificate of this kind could anything be moved out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When we were talking about relationships before the outbreak of the conflict in Kozarac itself, relationships with your neighbours, who were predominantly Muslim -- let me mention just a few names of those neighbours: Kahrimanovic, Adem; Beslagic; Arna- autovic, Shefik. Then there was a neighbour Peter Grahovac and some others. They were all elderly people, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the relations between Dusko Tadic and them? Were the relations normal or were they close friends?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With some of them he was friends and with others he had good neighbourly relations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With Shefik Arnautovic he was a friend, and the others were just neighbours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because after all he was younger than they, much younger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I should now like to refer to your husband's interests. You knew each other since you were 15?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have a hobby and what was his hobby?
