utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sports and painting, and we also did some mountaineering together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you accompany him in those activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I went for training with him. We went mountaineering. I didn't paint because I had absolutely no talent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wish to show you the newest painting your husband did. Do you recognise it? Please place it on the ELMO. This is the original?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin, the last exhibit, it's marked 114. The date on that, is that June 15th or 17th? The English says June 16th. I think we received one in evidence during trial that was June 15th. Is this 15th or 17th, not that it makes a difference, I suppose? If you look at the original, I don't know whether it was meant to be a 15 or 17 --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: I'm looking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour, no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Defence 114 then is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: You recognise who is on the painting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my daughter Alexandra.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your husband want to transform this hobby into an occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what way did he try to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The plan was if we had sufficient means of livelihood, then he would devote his full-time to his hobby.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your husband drink at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was an athlete.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he never drank alcohol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. On some occasions a glass or two, but in principle no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have any other hobbies, some other sports activities in addition to karate? Did he ride a bicycle or a motorbike? Did he ever use a motorbike?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can he ride a motorbike?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he can't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, in your opinion, after everything that has happened, could your husband, Mr. Dusko Tadic, return to Kozarac, Prijedor and Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because he's considered a deserter. He didn't respond to his military call-up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Any cross, Mr. ..

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Tadic, you are excused permanently. Thank you for coming again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (Witness withdrew from court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin, would you call your next witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Defence counsel calls Ms. Ljubica Metselaar, who will be examined by Mr. Livingston. Ms. Ljubica Metselaar (sworn) Examined by Mr. Livingston

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Ms. Metselaar, would you please take the oath that is being given to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's in Yugoslavian. Should I read it in Yugoslavian?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You should have your choice. There should be an English version. You should read either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Ms. Metselaar, just before we start your evidence properly, can I just remind you that although you and I are going to speak to each other in English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the sake of others, including Mr. Tadic, your evidence will be translated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So take it slowly, otherwise we will cause a panic up in the translation room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is your full name Ljubica Metselaar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just so the record is correct, that's spelt M-E-T-S-E-L-A-A-R?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think that you live in Rhenen in Holland; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which is about 100 kms south of here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're a Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were born in Bosnia in the town of Bosanski Brod; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which is just on the Serbian side of the Sava River?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think it's also right that when you were eight months old your parents left Bosanski Brod and went to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was there that you were brought up and went to school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You then left Yugoslavia I think in 1990-1991 and you went initially to England, and after you had met your husband to be, you came to Holland; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You married him in 1972?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've been here ever since?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's also correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as far as Mr. Tadic is concerned, is it correct that you never met him before he arrived in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never knew him before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Although I think you had heard of him through friends of yours in Germany?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My relative, my family in Germany. I heard when he was arrested in Germany.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your first contact with him was when you visited him in prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were you interested in doing that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, at the time it was still a war in Yugoslavia. He was the one, the first one who was arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt. I think to put a timescale on it, because I think the court may want that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was in 1994, about February 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that was, I think, when he was arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when he was arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I heard about it and then -- since then, better to say, started a propaganda against him all over the world. Everybody accused him of everything. Everybody hang him already without any proof, without any trial, without anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So when he was brought to Holland and to the Hague, I heard about it and I heard about a terrible condition that he's in, and then I got the thought he's my Serb. He's my Bosnia. He must be awfully lonely with the public opinion so against him, with the awful conditions that he was brought into, and he has nobody to talk to. He has no family. He has no relatives. He has no friends here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He must be suffering awfully. So I decided I will go there and I'll see for myself what kind of a man he is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I'll see if I can help him in any way just to ease the condition he's in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. So I think you obtained permission to see him from the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you went to see him, I think I'm right in saying, for the first time in September 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get on when you first met him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. From the first time on I found him a very nice man. He was awfully nervous with the first meeting; so did I. So we talked just a little bit and I told him why I came to see him, what was my motivation to see him, and I asked him if he need something, does he need anything that I can buy him and bring him, and he told me that he's not allowed to get any food from outside the prison. What I can bring him, if I want to, it's writing paper, some stamps, some pencils and those things, you know, that he can communicate with his family and write to his family if it is possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So I done it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll come to that a little bit later, Ms. Metselaar, but what did he talk to you about on that first occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, first of all, when I arrived for the first time, he told me: "I don't know if you are going to believe me, but I'm really not guilty of anything". So I told him: "Okay. I didn't come here to judge you. I came just as a friend".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he talk to you about in relation to his personal life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About his personal life, he showed me a picture of his family. That was a picture where his two daughters, his wife and his mother were standing in front of his house, and with tears in his eyes he said: "I don't know if I'm going to see them ever again". It's a very difficult situation. I can't stand a man with tears in his eyes. So I just tried to comfort him at that point, and to tell him: "Maybe it's not so bad as you think. Just wait and see". I told him that he has a very nice family. That's about -- you know, that's about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was the first visit, and I think thereafter you started visiting him every fortnight or thereabouts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's about, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you would on occasions bring him clothes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that ever at his request?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that was not on his request. I told him that I have relatives in Munich, where he was arrested, and he asked me only if I can get in touch with them to contact the person who was responsible for his belongings, you know after he was arrested and his family left Munich, if they can contact him to collect his things and to send it to me, that I will be able to bring it to him. So I done it and I told him on the second time that I visited him that the man didn't take good care of his things. He said that he put them in a basement and he got water in the basement and all the things that he left behind were really ruined. So he was left with nothing. He had nothing to wear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think it was for that reason that you and others whom you have gathered together have bought him suits and shirts and socks and shoes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He has to have something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some of which, of course, he has worn throughout this trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Tell us a little bit about -- you got together a Yugoslav club, I think, as you call it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was that for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was, you know, at that point engaged with the Yugoslavian club in a village nearby, and I told them that I visited Dusko Tadic, that I found him in a rather poor condition, about the clothing and everything, and I told them that it will be very nice if they can, you know, give some money -- to collect some money and to bring it to me and I'll bring it to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I think you did that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I done it. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he ask you to do with the money?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I told him that I brought some money -- it was not a very big amount; I can't remember the exact amount -- but he told me: "I don't need anything. Will you please be so kind to find a way if you can send it to my wife and my children? I personally don't need anything".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Help us about this, if you will?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Help us about this, if you will?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have seen him now for over two years regularly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much does his family mean to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His family means everything to him, absolutely everything. He told me repeatedly on several occasions that he will give his life for them if it is necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How does he regard his wife?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He loves her dearly. He thinks that she is the best friend he ever had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about his -- he's got two young daughters, has he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One whom we heard from yesterday, who's 17?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other one is how old?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She's about 7, 8, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how has it affected him being separated from his wife and his daughters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is very terrible for him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What has he said about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He's suffering very much. Every time he's talking about them he gets tears in his eyes and he's awfully concerned how they managed. It was still a war situation in the beginning when we were -- we met each other, and he was very concerned how they managed in a war situation without him, without any support of him, that he is unable to help them in any way, and maybe they are suffering, maybe they are dying of hunger. He doesn't know anything. The connections were very difficult with Bosnia at that time. That's why he asked me if I can send -- manage to send the money, because there was no -- because of the, you know, boycott of Yugoslavia and Bosnia included there was no bank traffic in between. So it was not so very easy to send it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I think also in addition to the regular visits you have made, you have exchanged letters and telephone calls with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that regular?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rather regular, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you to help us on this as well. Has he responded to this obvious kindness which you have shown him? How has he responded to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he was very pleased with the visit that I made to him. He's very, very caring man. He never failed if I told him just about my life, you know, talking with him, that I have some celebration or that I have something, I get a Christmas card for him, I got a card for the New Year for him, I got a card for my birthday, for the birthday of my husband. The collection I done for him he asked me personally if I will give him the names and addresses of the people who gave the money for him. He sent them a personal card thanking them for, you know, the sacrifice that they made for him. He never failed to show his gratitude, you know, for very small things that you are doing for him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I think, moving on chronologically, in January 1996 his family came here for the first time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were responsible for them while they were here; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First time not. Second time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means putting them up and looking after them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right, and I brought them every day to The Hague to visit him. I stayed in The Hague and then take them back home. They were just a guest in my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us what other things he talks to you about or he has talked to you about over the last couple of years or so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What other matters has he talked to you about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he told me about his trial, his defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He told me all his worries. He told me all his joys.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were his joys?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very little, very little, but, you know, for example, he got permission at last to train and got a gym, you know, that he can enter and train, because he is a karate man, and he told me that he's very glad at last he can do something, you know, physically to keep up in a good condition, to keep a good condition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Uh-huh. What else does he do with his time while he is in prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he told me at one point that he started painting again. So I said "again?". "Yes," he said, "again", because it runs in his family I learn later on, that they are very good in painting. So I said "okay". He asked me if I can bring him some colours and some brushes and some material, if it's not too much trouble. I told him: "Okay. I'll see what I can do".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you did that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Done it and he started painting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you have seen a lot of his pictures and I think a lot of them have been sent to London now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Through me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Hopefully to be exhibited somewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think there's even one of this Tribunal room, is there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It's exactly the Tribunal. I recognise it immediately. It's an awful nice picture, you know, full of colours and nice to look at, and he was rather proud of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think it has their Honours in a featured position; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he's a good artist, is he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not very good in painting, you know. I can't speak about that, but everybody who does know something about, they give a very, very nice opinion about. I'm really touched with his paintings, you know, with how he presented, you know, parts of his life in prison, but I can't say that they're perfect or something like that. Somebody else done that and they are really very good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now you have, I know, had quite a bit of contact with his wife and family; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often have you seen them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whenever they are in Holland I saw them. I keep in touch, you know, with them by telephone. I keep in touch writing to each other. So ..

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I would like you to tell us from an independent source how is his predicament affecting Mira and his daughters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was awful difficult time for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, it was still a wartime in Yugoslavia. She was left with two young children, a woman alone in a war situation, you know, when it's panicking all over around, people moving from the houses. Their house was ruined, nothing left to live in. They were just fugitives somewhere else, living on very, very poor aid that they got as fugitives. It was awful difficult time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How is it now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's getting a little bit better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I meant how is it for the family in terms of him not being with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, they're missing him awfully. He's missing a lot of the parts of the lives of his children, because they are growing up and he would never know what happened and how they reacted in one part of their lives, if you know what I mean. He can't -- he's, you know, his thread was just broken and he is picking up pieces any time they come to visit him but a lot of that he can't see. They are suffering on one side and he's suffering on the other. He's imprisoned. They are locked up. They can't go on with their lives so easily being a woman, the wife and daughters of Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Valentina particularly? How has his imprisonment affected her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Valentina is in a very, very difficult age. She is old enough to understand a lot of things, not old to be able to deal with a lot of things. She heard about awful things said about her father. She's suffering deeply. The first time when she came to Holland she didn't want to talk about it. She didn't want to talk about her feelings. She was not able to express them. The second time when she was in my home I tried to speak with her, you know, just to ease up, just to open herself, to be able to talk about, and now she's very comfortable with me, so she's talking about her feelings, expressing how much she is missing her father, because, as I understand from her saying and from his saying, they were very, very good friends, not daughter and father. They went out together. He even interested -- got her interested in karate. They talk about everything, just like two friends. So she's missing him awfully. The younger one is still young. She talks about father. She wants to have him at home, but she doesn't have that deepness, if you know what I mean, of the feelings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I want you to help us about one other matter, if you can, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever discussed with him his general feeling about the war in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is his attitude to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, because --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Presently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because he's Bosnia -- you see, I left Bosnia when I was very young. I grew up in Serbia. It's not much difference, but still I wanted to ask him some things about his opinion about, and he told me that it is absolutely madness what happened in Bosnia, that it should never, never take place. He grew in Bosnia among the Serbian as well as the Croats as well as the Muslims. In a time when he was growing up there was no difference in between those three groups. We were all Bosnians and that's true. I know that. Suddenly it's some kind of madness that come into the people that they can't stand each other any more. He was awfully sad that it happened as it happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Has he discussed it with you, did he do anything when he was in Bosnia to alleviate that sadness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He told me that -- well, he helped some people, because he was posted of the certain post as a policeman, and he was engaged also with distributing of humanitarian aid, and he said -- you see, being Bosnia, as I am, and feeling Bosnia, as I am, I distributed that aid without absolutely any difference in between the groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I think that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "I gave it to those ones that they needed the most at that point of -- at that moment. They are all the same to me. They are all my friends in some way, being Bosnians. So if they need food, I can't refuse them that. If they need clothes, I can't refuse them".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he a strong character?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He's a very strong character, very strong character.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How does that show itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can't turn him around. You can't -- if he has, you know, some point of view that he knows that he's right, you can't make him to change his mind not very easy, if you know what I mean. You have to come with very, very good facts on the table that he will say then: "Okay. I'll think about it. If you're right, I'll tell you".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You seem to be saying he is a bit stubborn, frankly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he is stubborn as well, as all Bosnians are, me including.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These activities you were talking about with the humanitarian aid, that was assisting the Red Cross, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's Red Cross in Bosnia. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I want you to -- you've had the opportunity to assess him in a much more independent way than perhaps other witnesses who have given evidence today and yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's your assessment of his character?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in a few words, he is a rather caring, very sensitive man, nice man to talk to, easy talker, good listener, and a very, very, very lovely man to have around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know, as everybody else in this courtroom knows, even better than me that he has been convicted of some very serious crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do those -- are those crimes, as far as you are concerned and in your judgement of him, are they in character or are they out of character for him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think out of character. I can't match those -- knowing him, I can't match those two things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Ms. Metselaar. I don't know whether there will be any other questions for you, but there may be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Metselaar. You are permanently excused. Thank you for coming. You are now excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for listening. Okay. (Witness withdrew from court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin, would you call your next witness? Is it the Professor, or do we have more?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do have the Professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Pardon me?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are expecting Professor Zivojin Aleksic to appear before this court, as we proposed in our written submission, but we feel that perhaps it would be best to hear him tomorrow, but the Defence would like, in accordance with your ruling of June 12th, to submit to the court three further written statements in reference to what has been offered by the Prosecution in its written submission. This is evidence regarding the tax dues of the persons referred to in the written submission of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You say tax dues. I don't really know what they are. You may offer what you wish and then I'll rule on it after hearing the position of the Prosecutor, but you did --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: (Not translated).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You did hear the statement that I made when we began this proceedings and that is although there is mention of loss and a particular specific amount in the statements, the Trial Chamber is not concerned really with the exact dollar amount of the loss or any dollar amount. What we're concerned about is whether there is loss. So if that's what you're attempting to rebut, you, of course, may do so, but I don't think you should have much concern about the weight that will be given to that particular portion of the impact statements that we received, but why don't you have marked -- would you please, usher, take those and let's have them marked and then let's see what they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: If I may be permitted, I listened carefully to the statements of the Trial Chamber yesterday. We are not insisting on these sums. We just wish the Trial Chamber to have before it authentic documents indicating the kind of affairs these persons engaged in, the persons who claim damages, and whether they could have had such a degree of losses. We are not entering into the actual figures, but simply we wish you to have the ability to review these persons' capacity to acquire such high amounts of property and to suffer such high losses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, you have what has been marked for identification purposes as defence 116, 117 and 118. Have you had an opportunity to examine these and can you respond as to whether you have an objection me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I'm in a position to respond, and I do have those exhibits before me. We object to them, firstly, on the grounds that they are irrelevant. How a person organises their tax affairs and what position exists between them and the Tax Commissioner, whoever is responsible for Internal Revenue, can be totally different to what people's assets are and how those assets are held. In my submission this goes nowhere in assisting the Tribunal in any way in determining anything other than it's an attempt, in my submission -- other than it could be an attempt, in my submission, to somehow suggest that these people either were not paying their taxes and, therefore, are of some way bad character. If that's the basis on which it's put, then we object to it on that basis as well, but on the other basis, we submit that it's irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I'll overrule your objection. They will be admitted. Defence exhibits 116, 117 and 118 are admitted and will be given the appropriate weight. Mr. Vujin do you have anything additional other than Professor Aleksic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point in time the Defence has nothing more to say except to propose that we begin tomorrow with Professor Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: How long do you think you will need to elicit Professor Aleksic's testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, it's rather difficult to tell, because professors tend to speak at some length, but I think one to one and a half hours should be sufficient, or two academic hours. An hour, I think, will be enough probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: The Prosecution has indicated that they will need approximately two hours for their oral submissions on appropriate sentence. How many time do you think that you will need.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: The defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Maybe Mr. Niemann wants to correct me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I rise to say I did indicate that but I suspect it will be something lessor, shorter than that. Probably more like an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Very good. Mr. Vujin, how long would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: I think that we, too, could reduce this to two, two and a half hours in all for the statement of the whole defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Reduce it from what?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: To two hours. Two, two and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I was really determining we have tomorrow afternoon and then of course we have Thursday afternoon and then we will hear from Dr Nedopil on Friday. So we have enough time to complete, Mr. Niemann, using Wednesday afternoon, Thursday afternoon. Friday we will have the initial appearance at 10 o'clock and so I imagine we will not begin until 11 o'clock, but even starting at 11 o'clock on Friday, I'm positive we will have enough time to complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. So we will adjourn until --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Just to understand these documents that you have just submitted, I notice that one of them relates to 1990 and that's the second one you submitted, without naming names, and it refers to the exchange rate of a Dinar at that time as being 7 Dinars to the Deutsch Mark. The income there is shown as 25,000 Dinars. Then in the year before it is shown as 3 million and a few hundred thousand Dinars. Was the exchange rate very different in 1989 than it was in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, Judge Stephen. It was substantially different. The exchange rate for the Dinar, it was devalued. A certain number of zeros were taken off. In relation to the Deutsch Mark, the exchange rate changed, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: So there wasn't equation of continuing inflation, but rather the contrary; the Dinar became -- was re-organised and became very much more valuable in 1990, did it, the new Dinar?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. Before that there was soaring inflation, and then in 1990 it was halted and the inflation rate was fixed to the Deutsch Mark 1:7 and it was stable for a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Then in subsequent years, 1993 and 1994, it again soared, didn't it, as far as inflation?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, one can't even talk about the value of the Dinar. It was impossible to follow it. At the time the conflict broke out in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, the Dinar had one value at 9 o'clock in the morning and a different one at 1.00 pm. That was our tragedy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the one remaining issue was the complete psychiatric report and whether it was going to be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: We have received the psychiatric report. What exhibit is that, Mr. Bos? Is that an exhibit or was that just provided to us? Have you had an opportunity to examine the translation of the entire report of Dr Nedopil?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I received this copy an hour ago from Mr. Keegan in English and I really had no time to compare. I have no doubts regarding the translation, but I would like to have the opportunity until tomorrow to make a comparison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That's acceptable. We will then hear from you tomorrow at 2.30 regarding that report, and that should be admitted into evidence if he is going to speak orally on Friday. We will adjourn then until 2.30 tomorrow. (5.20 pm)
